inlines.text: 【X 长文】Getting started with Claude Code Mods

blocks.text: Mods were released in Claude Code a few weeks ago, and I'm sharing this guide to make it easier to get started with them.

inlines.text: Mods were released in Claude Code a few weeks ago, and I'm sharing this guide to make it easier to get started with them.

blocks.text: Mods are small JavaScript or TypeScript files that you run within your Claude Code session. They allow you to react to events, modify the behavior of Claude Code or render your own interfaces in both the terminal and desktop applications. Here's a nice ~3m video on mods by Lydia:

blocks.text: What I love most about mods is that they can be created without learning their API. Run claude and describe the mod you want it to create. Approve the files as Claude writes them, say yes when asked to enable hot reloading, and your mod will be shown when the turn ends.

blocks.text: In this guide, you'll find a high-level overview of the capabilities of mods and how to prompt Claude Code to create one. You'll also learn how to persist, distribute and install your own mods. Btw, a more code-heavy version of this write-up is available too but also just ask Claude to help build your mods.

blocks.text: While Claude Code already lets you customize a lot of its behavior, such as configuration settings, permission policies, slash commands, skills and status lines, mods allow you to do so much more. With mods you can alter or override the behavior of Claude Code or render your own custom interfaces. Folks have been having fun building mods, including multiplayer Doom!

blocks.text: For our walkthrough we'll begin with Token Weather, a mod that displays a turn-by-turn forecast of the context window above the prompt. Then we'll look at two more complex mods, Blast Radius and Replay Theater, to explore the possibilities of mods further.

blocks.text: How mods work

inlines.text: How mods work

blocks.text: At a technical level, mods are hooks bundled with plugins. Each hook can see all events occurring within the session, such as when tool calls are made, prompts are submitted, turns start and end, sessions start and end, slash commands are executed, and every rendering of any part of the UI.

inlines.text: At a technical level, mods are hooks bundled with plugins. Each hook can see all events occurring within the session, such as when tool calls are made, prompts are submitted, turns start and end, sessions start and end, slash commands are executed, and every rendering of any part of the UI.

blocks.text: Hooks are chained together like middleware. When an event occurs, it is passed through your hook, then through other plugins, before finally hitting Claude Code and performing its default action.

inlines.text: Hooks are chained together like middleware. When an event occurs, it is passed through your hook, then through other plugins, before finally hitting Claude Code and performing its default action.

blocks.text: A hook can do one of three things when an event occurs:

inlines.text: A hook can do one of three things when an event occurs:

blocks.text: - Observe: Allow the event to continue and observe the outcome. For instance, a hook could log every time a file is modified or take a snapshot after every turn.

inlines.text: - Observe: Allow the event to continue and observe the outcome. For instance, a hook could log every time a file is modified or take a snapshot after every turn.

blocks.text: - Rewrite: Change the event for the remaining hooks. For instance, a hook could add text to a prompt or change a tool call's input.

inlines.text: - Rewrite: Change the event for the remaining hooks. For instance, a hook could add text to a prompt or change a tool call's input.

blocks.text: - Answer: Handle the event itself, so the default behavior doesn't run. For instance, a hook could deny a tool call or answer a command.

inlines.text: - Answer: Handle the event itself, so the default behavior doesn't run. For instance, a hook could deny a tool call or answer a command.

blocks.text: These terms are helpful when thinking about what a mod does and how to ask Claude for one: "Refuse this kind of command" is an answer, whereas "Take a snapshot after every turn" is an observation.

inlines.text: These terms are helpful when thinking about what a mod does and how to ask Claude for one: "Refuse this kind of command" is an answer, whereas "Take a snapshot after every turn" is an observation.

blocks.text: What makes mods different from settings hooks

inlines.text: What makes mods different from settings hooks

blocks.text: A settings hook is a shell command that runs each time an event occurs. A mod is loaded once into a session and maintains its own state and UI which it can update in response to events. A mod can also call back into Claude Code. For example, it can open a pane, spawn a process, or register a slash command or tool that's callable by the model.

inlines.text: A settings hook is a shell command that runs each time an event occurs. A mod is loaded once into a session and maintains its own state and UI which it can update in response to events. A mod can also call back into Claude Code. For example, it can open a pane, spawn a process, or register a slash command or tool that's callable by the model.

blocks.text: We use mods to implement some of Claude Code's own features, such as AGENTS.md support and the /diff pane. The code and tests are available in the public anthropics/claude-code repo in the mods/ directory.

blocks.text: Write your first mod: Token Weather

inlines.text: Write your first mod: Token Weather

blocks.text: Token Weather tells you how full the context window is, after each turn, by displaying one line in the band above the prompt that includes a weather icon and the percentage of the context window that's used. It also displays how many tokens have been used from the context window, a miniature chart showing the progression of the context window over the last few turns, and how many tokens have been added since the last turn.

It also displays how many tokens have been used from the context window, a miniature chart showing the progression of the context window over the last few turns, and how many tokens have been added since the last turn.

blocks.text: You'll notice the prompt never mentions events, state or the API. It only says what you want to see. Claude Code ships with a guide for writing mods, so it already knows the how: where to keep state so a reload doesn't wipe it, how to check the plugin with claude plugin validate, which events to hook.

blocks.text: Staying around

inlines.text: Staying around

blocks.text: A mod built this way only loads for the current session, and its folder gets cleaned up later. To hold on to it, copy the folder out of ~/.claude/dev-mods/<session-id>/ and install it like any other plugin, which the next section covers.

blocks.text: Publishing and installing mods

inlines.text: Publishing and installing mods

blocks.text: Mods are just Claude Code plugins, so publishing and installing them is the same as with any other plugin. To publish a mod, just put it in a GitHub repo and include a marketplace file in it; that will make it a marketplace you can publish to, and you can push updates to it in the usual way.

inlines.text: Mods are just Claude Code plugins, so publishing and installing them is the same as with any other plugin. To publish a mod, just put it in a GitHub repo and include a marketplace file in it; that will make it a marketplace you can publish to, and you can push updates to it in the usual way.

blocks.text: To install a mod, use three commands in Claude Code:

inlines.text: To install a mod, use three commands in Claude Code:

blocks.text: - /plugin marketplace add the GitHub repo (e.g. your-org/my-mods)

inlines.text: - /plugin marketplace add the GitHub repo (e.g. your-org/my-mods)

blocks.text: - /plugin install the mod name from that marketplace (e.g. token-weather@my-mods), then pick a scope

inlines.text: - /plugin install the mod name from that marketplace (e.g. token-weather@my-mods), then pick a scope

blocks.text: - /reload-plugins if the mod doesn't start on its own

blocks.text: Safety

inlines.text: Safety

blocks.text: Mods are code that runs within Claude Code on your local machine, with your permissions. Mods aren't sandboxed: they can read your files and secrets, start processes, make network requests and approve tool calls. Mods are written by their author, not Anthropic.

inlines.text: Mods are code that runs within Claude Code on your local machine, with your permissions. Mods aren't sandboxed: they can read your files and secrets, start processes, make network requests and approve tool calls. Mods are written by their author, not Anthropic.

blocks.text: As you would with any package, read the source and only install mods from people you trust. To see what a mod hooks and calls before you install it, run claude plugin validate on its folder.

inlines.text: As you would with any package, read the source and only install mods from people you trust. To see what a mod hooks and calls before you install it, run claude plugin validate on its folder.

blocks.text: Blast Radius intercepts calls from Claude to Bash that are potentially dangerous (e.g. rm -rf, git reset --hard, git clean, force push, database migration) and calculates what they would do. A pane opens with a Proceed or Cancel button.

blocks.text: If the terminal is wide enough, the pane docks on the side next to the transcript. If not, Blast Radius renders the report above the prompt. Only one mod can use that band at a time, so if another mod holds it the buttons may not appear, and the command is refused after 10 minutes.

blocks.text: Think of this as a safety net rather than a real firewall. It reads the command text, so $(…), aliases and scripts that call rm will get past it. If you want a hard block, use permission rules.

blocks.text: Replay Theater: reviewing what happened at the end of the turn

inlines.text: Replay Theater: reviewing what happened at the end of the turn

blocks.text: When a turn is running, Replay Theater watches all of the Edit and Write calls to see which files changed and what they changed to. At the end of a turn, you can see a message above the prompt to let you know that you can replay them. Type /replay (or press ctrl+x then Tab to focus the band, then r) and you'll see a pane that'll show the changes for each edit with diffs. It'll have a list of the step numbers and Prev, Next and Close buttons.

At the end of a turn, you can see a message above the prompt to let you know that you can replay them. Type /replay (or press ctrl+x then Tab to focus the band, then r) and you'll see a pane that'll show the changes for each edit with diffs. It'll have a list of the step numbers and Prev, Next and Close buttons.

blocks.text: It never blocks or affects edits, it just watches.

inlines.text: It never blocks or affects edits, it just watches.

blocks.text: Each turn gets its own replay, and subagent edits are included in the main turn's replay. Where the pane goes depends on the space: it's docked on the right in fullscreen and inline above the prompt at 80 columns.
